patch.value: The project shipped 68 releases and none of them exists in its own relationship graph, so the timeline the record is supposed to explain is reachable only by grouping a scalar

Measured 2026-08-11 across all 2,437 items.

1,782 items carry a release value and 68 distinct release identities appear. The values are totally ordered by construction, because this project's versions are date-based. Every item that shipped therefore knows which epoch carried it, and the epochs know their own order.

None of that is in the graph.

release is a scalar string on an item. The schema declares 17 item types and not one of them denotes a release, an epoch, or a shipped increment. The graph holds ten edge kinds and not one of them relates an item to the release that carried it, or one release to the release before it.

Every consequence is a traversal question the record cannot answer:

what shipped in v2026.8.9 is a group-by over a string field, not a neighbourhood, so it costs a full-corpus scan and returns no structure;

which release preceded v2026.8.9 requires parsing the version identifier, and that parse is the only ordering the project has;

which release introduced the defect an item fixes has no path at all, because the fixing item and the introducing item are joined only through prose;

what a release inherited as open blockers from its predecessor cannot be computed, because the boundary between two epochs is not a node a traversal can stop at.

The gap is visible in the project's own exemplars. The bundled vcs-exemplar extension registers Changeset and VcsRef item types, so modelling a version-control epoch as a first-class node is demonstrated for a foreign domain and left unused for this project's own releases.

This is the missing dimension for every consumer that wants to read the record as a history rather than as a set. Point-in-time projection, evolution traversal, throughput forecasting and the changelog all currently derive the epoch from a mutable timestamp or from a string, which is also why release attribution and changelog ordering keep drifting.

The epoch representation must stay derived. A hand-maintained release ledger would be a fourth ledger to disagree with the three the project already keeps.

A release epoch is representable as a first-class node with a declared type, so epoch membership and epoch order are edges rather than a scalar plus a version parse; Every item carrying a release value is joined to its epoch by a typed edge, and the join is derived from the recorded value rather than asserted item by item; Consecutive epochs carry a typed ordering edge, so a traversal reconstructs the full release sequence without interpreting version identifiers; Traversal answers what shipped in a named release and which release preceded it, and both are bounded reads rather than full-corpus group-bys; Items with no release value appear as a named residual population rather than being silently excluded, so a shipped but unstamped item is visible; The epoch representation is derived and reproducible from the immutable record alone, so it never becomes a fourth release ledger to disagree with the three that already exist

message: Filed from a release-epoch census: 68 epochs, 1782 stamped items, zero epoch nodes

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Quantifying the layer this item would add, measured 2026-08-13.

Shortest-path depth from the seven apex nodes over the full edge basis, computed inward across all recorded edges: depth 0 holds 7, depth 1 holds 492, depth 2 holds 1,464, depth 3 holds 488, depth 4 holds 16, and nothing is deeper. So 59 percent of the entire corpus sits exactly two hops from an apex and the graph bottoms out at four.

That is the structural reason a timeline question is hard to ask here, and it is not a linking deficiency that more edges would fix. The layers that would make the record deep are the entities the project already has and has never made nodes of. Releases are the largest: 68 of them, each with a known membership, each sitting between a tranche of work and the outcome it advanced. Adding them inserts a real layer everywhere — terminal task, tranche, release, outcome — rather than an invented one, and it does so for the whole closed population at once, which is the part of the corpus that currently attaches most shallowly.

The companion measurement worth carrying into the design: today the release relation is expressible only by grouping a scalar, so the 1,770 closed items that carry a release value are joined to each other by string equality and to nothing by an edge, while the 337 that carry none are joined to nothing at all.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Re-measured 2026-08-30, and the population this item describes has grown rather than shrunk: 1,787 of 2,602 items now carry a release value across 70 distinct releases, up from 1,782 of 2,437 across 68. The 815 items with no release value are the named residual population the acceptance criteria require to stay visible.

Two independent measurements taken today argue that this item, not another enrichment wave, is the correct next instrument for the graph programme.

First, the ordering dimension is the only unsaturated one left. Counting each node once if it carries any edge of a family in either direction, 2,600 of 2,602 items carry a semantic edge while only 474 carry an ordering edge, so the semantic families are at 99.92 percent coverage and sequence is at 18.2 percent. The full measurement is recorded on pm-gxs55a.

Second, the epoch spine is recoverable without inventing anything. The 70 release identities are totally ordered by construction because the versions are date-based, and each item's membership is already a recorded scalar. A derived projection therefore adds 70 nodes and roughly 1,787 membership edges plus 69 succession edges to the ordering dimension from data the record already holds, which would take sequence coverage from 18.2 percent to above 88 percent and give the longest ordering chain a floor of 70 rather than its current 10.

The constraint in the acceptance criteria remains the design's load-bearing part and is worth restating for whoever implements it: the epoch representation must be derived and reproducible from the immutable record, never materialized as items. Hand-creating 70 release documents would satisfy every traversal criterion above and simultaneously violate the last one, because it would become the fourth release ledger to disagree with the three that already exist. That is also why this was left as a projection rather than executed as a backfill during this session's graph pass.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Derived release-epoch projection, design recorded 2026-09-12 so the acceptance criteria can be built as a read-time projection rather than as stored items.

Why not stored items. Materialising one item per release plus one edge per stamped item would create about ninety new nodes and 1787 edges that duplicate the release scalar, and the sixth criterion forbids exactly that: a fourth release ledger that can disagree with npm, git tags and the changelog. Epochs must be derived from the immutable record on every read and be byte-reproducible.

Node derivation. For each distinct non-empty release value across all items, emit a virtual node with id release:<value>, type ReleaseEpoch, and the membership set of item ids whose release field equals the value. Items with no release value form the residual node release:unstamped, partitioned by lifecycle role (active, terminal) so a shipped but unstamped item is visible as the fifth criterion requires. Node identity is the literal stamp; no version parsing is involved.

Ordering derivation, in precedence order and without interpreting version identifiers. First, the recorded cut events: the release pipeline's version commit and the history entries that stamp release values carry timestamps, so the first stamp event per release value in the union of history streams gives a total order that reproduces from the record alone. Second, when two values share a first-stamp timestamp (bulk backfills), break the tie by the earliest closed_at among members. Third, values that appear only through a backfill with identical timestamps and no closed_at are reported unordered rather than guessed, as an explicit finding. Consecutive nodes in that order carry the ordering edge kind precedes; the current open epoch is the residual node's active partition.

Membership edges. Each member item is joined to its epoch by shipped_in, source item, target epoch, derived at read time; the reverse direction is answered by the epoch node's member list. The edge carries derivation source release_field so a later correction supersedes instead of overwriting.

Reads. pm graph epochs lists the ordered epochs with member counts and the residual; pm graph successors release:<v> and predecessors answer which release preceded which; pm graph descendants release:<v> answers what shipped in a named release; all are bounded by the existing row and token dimensions and never group the whole corpus at the CLI layer. pm graph audit gains epoch_count, ordered_epoch_count, unordered_epoch_count and unstamped_terminal_count in its profile so the residual is a governance metric.

Cost and scale. One pass over item metadata (already cached) to bucket by release value, O(n); ordering from the history index is O(number of releases) once the first-stamp table is built and cached under the same signature as the metadata cache. At a million items and thousands of releases the epoch table stays small and the member lists are served as cursors.

Verification. Property: for every stamped item, exactly one shipped_in edge and its epoch's member list contains it. Negative control: a workspace with no release values yields only the residual node and zero precedes edges. Reproducibility: two reads of the same commit produce identical bytes. Consumers: the changelog generator can check its section order against the derived order (pm-q91qyd, pm-pcys9n), and the relevance engine consumes epoch distance as catalog entry (48) on pm-4k6b.
